title: Bit Manipulation
relevance: Bit manipulation is asked because it is essential for high-performance computing, cryptography, and solving specific algorithmic constraints optimally when everyday abstractions are not enough.

phases.goal: Establish binary representation, two's complement, and the six bitwise operators plus core one-liner idioms.

must_hit.point: In a standard C++ environment an int is a 32-bit signed integer using two's complement, where the 31st bit (zero-indexed from the right) is the sign bit.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states 32-bit int, two's complement, and that the sign bit is the 31st bit (0 positive, 1 negative).

must_hit.point: To negate in two's complement: invert all bits with bitwise NOT, then add 1.
C++ has six fundamental bitwise operators: & (AND), | (OR), ^ (XOR), ~ (NOT), << (left shift), and >> (right shift); left shift is mathematically equivalent to multiplying by a power of 2.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists the six operators and links << to multiply-by-power-of-2.

must_hit.point: Core idioms: set i-th bit with x | (1 << i), clear with x & ~(1 << i), toggle with x ^ (1 << i), check with (x >> i) & 1, lowest set bit with x & -x, remove lowest set bit with x & (x - 1).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recalls several table idioms accurately, especially set/clear/toggle/check and x & (x - 1) / x & -x.

probes: Walk through how a signed int is stored in two's complement and name the six bitwise operators with what each does.
What one-liner sets, clears, toggles, or checks the i-th bit?

hints.1: Think about the sign bit and how negation is formed from NOT.
hints.3: 32-bit two's complement uses the 31st bit as sign; negate via ~ then +1; idioms are x|(1<<i), x&~(1<<i), x^(1<<i), (x>>i)&1.

phases.goal: Show how bit idioms compose into O(1) checks and Kernighan-style loops for set-bit work.

must_hit.point: Check the i-th bit by shifting right by i then AND with 1: ((n >> k) & 1) != 0.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains bring bit to position 0 then isolate with & 1.

must_hit.point: A number is a power of 2 iff n > 0 and (n & (n - 1)) == 0, because that expression drops the lowest set bit and a power of 2 has exactly one set bit.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States both the n > 0 guard and the (n & (n - 1)) == 0 check with the one-set-bit rationale.

must_hit.point: Brian Kernighan's popcount repeatedly does n = n & (n - 1) until n is 0; iteration count equals the number of set bits, in O(k) time where k is the number of set bits.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes clearing the lowest set bit each step and counting until zero.

must_hit.point: Oddness is (n & 1) != 0 because the 0-th bit is 1 for odd integers; even is (x & 1) == 0.

probes: How do you test power-of-two in O(1) without looping divides by 2?
Explain Brian Kernighan's algorithm versus shifting through all bits.

hints.1: Relate n & (n - 1) to clearing the lowest set bit.
hints.2: Power of two has exactly one set bit; popcount loops that clear until zero.
hints.3: isPowerOfTwo: n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0; Kernighan: while n: n &= n-1; count++.

phases.goal: Contrast production vs interview bit techniques and when bitmask enumeration is the right subset tool.

must_hit.point: For counting set bits in competitive programming prefer __builtin_popcount (often a single hardware instruction) over a manual Kernighan loop.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says use the builtin/intrinsic in CP rather than hand-rolled popcount.

must_hit.point: XOR swap without an extra variable is mostly an interview curiosity; in production always use std::swap.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Acknowledges XOR swap works via self-inverse XOR but prefers std::swap in real code.

must_hit.point: Bitmask power-set enumeration is elegant, but backtracking is often preferred when subsets must be generated in a specific lexicographical order.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts mask-from-0-to-2^n-1 with backtracking for ordered subset generation.

probes: When would you use __builtin_popcount instead of Brian Kernighan's loop?
Bitmask subsets versus backtracking—when do you prefer each?

hints.1: Think interview demo versus what you ship or need ordered.
hints.2: Intrinsics vs O(k) loop; mask enumeration vs lex-order backtracking; XOR swap vs std::swap.
hints.3: CP: __builtin_popcount; production swap: std::swap; ordered subsets: often backtracking over pure bitmasks.

phases.goal: Apply XOR cancellation, bit-diff popcount, range XOR, bitmask subsets, and safe division-by-shifts to classic interview problems.

must_hit.point: Minimum bit flips from start to goal is the popcount of start ^ goal (XOR marks differing bits).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Computes start ^ goal then counts set bits (e.g. Kernighan).

must_hit.point: Single Number I: XOR all elements; duplicates cancel (XOR self-inverse), leaving the unique value in O(n) time and O(1) space.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Accumulates ^= across the array and cites pair annihilation.

must_hit.point: Power set: n elements yield 2^n subsets; iterate mask from 0 to 2^n - 1 and include i if (mask >> i) & 1, in O(n · 2^n) time and space.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes mask loop and bit test to build each subset.

must_hit.point: XOR of [L, R] is f(R) ^ f(L - 1) where f(n) is XOR of 1..n and depends on n % 4 (0→n, 1→1, 2→n+1, 3→0).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses prefix XOR identity and the four-case mod-4 formula.

must_hit.point: Single Number III: XOR all to get X ^ Y, take lowest set bit (xorAll & -xorAll), partition into two buckets by that bit, XOR each bucket to isolate X and Y.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates by a differing bit of the two uniques after full XOR.

must_hit.point: Divide without * / % by shifting the divisor to the largest fitting multiple of a power of 2, subtracting, and accumulating; handle dividend == INT_MIN && divisor == -1 by returning INT_MAX, and use long long to avoid shift UB.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes shift-and-subtract quotient building plus the INT_MIN/-1 and long long safeguards.

probes: How do you find the single number when every other value appears twice?
Generate all subsets with bitmasks—what is the mask range and how do you test membership?
Two uniques appear once and others twice—how do you recover both in O(1) extra space?

hints.1: XOR cancels pairs; differing bits are exactly where XOR is 1.
hints.2: Flips: popcount(start^goal); subsets: masks 0..2^n-1; two uniques: split on lowest set bit of total XOR.
hints.3: result ^= num for Single Number I; for III use lowestSetBit = xorAll & -xorAll then two buckets; range XOR via xor1ToN(r)^xor1ToN(l-1) with n%4 cases.

tradeoffs.topic: Brian Kernighan popcount vs naive shift-by-1 loop
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Kernighan clears one set bit per iteration so time is O(k) in the number of set bits; interviewers contrast this with a naive loop that shifts through all bits. In competitive programming, prefer __builtin_popcount, which often compiles to a single hardware instruction.

Bitmasks map each subset to a mask from 0 to 2^n - 1 and extract bits in O(n · 2^n); elegant for full power sets, but backtracking is often preferred when subsets must appear in a specific lexicographical order.
Chained XOR exploits X^X=0 and X^0=X to swap without an extra variable, but it is mostly an interview curiosity; in production code always use std::swap.

gotchas.correction: & , | , and ^ have lower precedence than == / !=, so n & 1 == 0 parses as n & (1 == 0). Always write (n & 1) == 0.

gotchas.trap: Left-shifting a negative signed integer, or shifting by a count >= width (e.g. 1 << 32 on a 32-bit int)
gotchas.correction: These invoke Undefined Behavior in C++. Convert to a wider type such as long long before aggressive shifts, and never shift by >= bit width.

gotchas.trap: Dividing INT_MIN by -1 or shifting toward the sign bit during divide-without-operators
gotchas.correction: INT_MIN / -1 overflows a 32-bit int (INT_MAX + 1); return INT_MAX. Operate on long long absolutes so left shifts do not hit sign-bit UB.

gotchas.trap: Claiming n & (n - 1) == 0 alone proves power of two
gotchas.correction: Also require n > 0; non-positive numbers cannot be powers of 2 even if the bit idiom looks plausible.

gotchas.trap: Computing lowest set bit as xorAll & -xorAll on a plain int when xorAll could be INT_MIN
gotchas.correction: Cast to long long before xorAll & -xorAll to avoid UB on INT_MIN when isolating the lowest set bit for Single Number III.
